citation.title: Estimating Causal Effects in Experiments with Network Spillovers

standing_assumptions:
[Nature of the work] The chapter (chapter 16 of the Handbook of Computational Social Science; printed pp. 209–222, PDF pp. 1–14, printed page = PDF page + 208) is an exposition with worked R examples. It has no numbered theorem, proposition, lemma, assumption or proof and no displayed estimator; its two mathematical displays are the exposure mapping (p. 211) and the estimand (p. 212). Note 2 (p. 221, PDF p. 13): “For a formal discussion of the estimators, see Aronow and Samii (2017).” Everything quoted below was read from the page images.
(S1) Population and network. p. 210 (PDF p. 2): “We imagine a situation where an analyst is planning an experiment on a finite population, $U$, of units indexed by $i = 1,...,N$. The units are connected to each other through a network that we represent as an $N \times N$ adjacency matrix, $\theta$, with entries that equal, for example, 0 or 1 (and with 0’s on the diagonal). A value of 1 in row $i$ and column $j$ in the adjacency matrix means that $i$’s potential outcomes might depend on whether or not $j$ is treated (e.g., they may be immediate peers or close to each other in the network). A value of 0 in row $i$ and column $j$ means that $i$’s potential outcomes most certainly do not depend on $j$’s treatment status (e.g., there are no channels through which $j$ could influence $i$, even indirectly). The undirected network in Figure 16.1 would be represented by a symmetric adjacency matrix, with 1’s representing edges between units and 0’s representing the absence of edges.”
(S2) Treatment and design. pp. 210–211 (PDF pp. 2–3): “The experiment is one in which units could be assigned to either a “treatment” or “control” condition. We use an indicator, $z_i \in \{0,1\}$, to denote whether unit $i$ is assigned to treatment ($z_i = 1$) or control $z_i = 0$). The $N \times 1$ vector of treatments for all units is given by $\mathbf{z} = (z_1,...,z_N)'$. Given that treatments are binary, there are, in principle, $2^N$ different treatment assignment profiles that could be constructed. An experimental design assigns some probability, $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, to a treatment profile, $\mathbf{z}$. Under the Bernoulli assignment experimental design, treatments are assigned through independent Bernoulli draws (e.g., independent coin flips), in which case $p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0$ for any of the $2^N$ possible profiles, although $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ would be vanishingly small for some profiles (such as the profile in which $\mathbf{z}$ is a vector of only 0’s). The complete random assignment design, in which $N_1$ units are randomly assigned (without replacement) to treatment and $N_0 = N - N_1$ units to control, yields $p_{\mathbf{z}} = 0$ for any assignment in which more or fewer than $N_1$ units are assigned to treatment, and $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ would otherwise be uniform for all assignments with $N_1$ units assigned to treatment. Other types of experimental designs include various forms of stratified and clustered designs. Let the random $N \times 1$ vector $\mathbf{Z}$ refer to the treatment assignment profile that is ultimately realized, with $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$.”
(S3) Potential outcomes. p. 211 (PDF p. 3): “We define causal effects in terms of how units’ potential outcomes would change as $\mathbf{z}$ changes (Imbens & Rubin, 2015, ch. 1–2). We denote $i$’s potential outcome under treatment assignment vector $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i(\mathbf{z})$, where $y_i(\cdot)$ is a real-valued function that maps treatment profiles to an individual’s outcome. For unit $i$, the effect of applying treatment profile $\mathbf{z}$ as compared to $\mathbf{z}'$ would be measured in the way that $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ differs from $y_i(\mathbf{z}')$. We focus on effects defined as differences, such as $y_i(\mathbf{z}) - y_i(\mathbf{z}')$.”
(S4) Exposure mapping. p. 211 (PDF p. 3): “Following the approach of Aronow and Samii (2017), we define an exposure mapping, $f(\cdot)$, to establish what we think is the plausible extent and nature of spillover. For a unit $i$, the exposure mapping takes a treatment profile, $\mathbf{z}$, from the experimental design and the interference network, $\theta$, as inputs, and then as an output, it generates an exposure, $d$. The exposure mapping is a way of modeling how different patterns of treatment assignment among peers might induce different potential outcomes. Thus, the exposure mapping translates potential outcomes defined in terms of treatment profiles, $\mathbf{z}$, into potential outcomes defined in terms of exposures, $d$. For example, we might suppose that a given unit’s potential outcomes depend on whether (a) they are treated or (b) any one of their network peers is treated. This would imply an exposure mapping that takes as inputs the assignment profile $\mathbf{z}$ and unit $i$’s row in the adjacency matrix, $\theta_i$, as follows: $$f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = \begin{cases} d_{11}\ (\text{Direct + Indirect Exposure}): & z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1, \\ d_{10}\ (\text{Isolated Direct Exposure}): & z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1, \\ d_{01}\ (\text{Indirect Exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1, \\ d_{00}\ (\text{No Exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1 \end{cases}$$ This particular exposure mapping implies that each unit $i$ has four potential outcomes, $(y_i(d_{11}), y_i(d_{10}), y_i(d_{01}), y_i(d_{00}))$, which are based on combinations of their own treatment status and whether any of their peers is treated.” (The last clause is on p. 212, PDF p. 4. The display prints the four labels without spaces between words. The product $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$ is as printed; see P044-T9.)
(S5) Estimand. p. 212 (PDF p. 4): “These exposure-based potential outcomes define causal effects. Under the exposure mapping defined above, the effect for unit $i$ of being treated along with their peers, as compared to being in a situation where neither the unit nor any of their peers are treated, is given by $y_i(d_{11}) - y_i(d_{00})$ . Insofar as this effect differs from the effect of isolated direct exposure ($y_i(d_{10}) - y_i(d_{00})$), then network spillover effects are meaningful in altering outcomes for those who are directly treated. Once the treatment profile, $\mathbf{Z}$, is drawn, units will be assigned to the corresponding exposure, $d$, and will reveal the associated potential outcome, $y_i(d)$. For a given unit, other exposures are counterfactual and not directly observable. For this reason, we do not focus on trying to estimate unit-level effects, but rather on average effects for the entire population, $$\tau(d,d') = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i(d) - y_i(d')),$$ where $d$ and $d'$ are two different possible exposures.”
(S6) The recipe for exposure probabilities. p. 212 (PDF p. 4): “Moreover, with the network adjacency matrix and exposure mapping in hand, these probabilities of exposure can be computed directly from the experimental design. Specifically, one can simulate treatment assignments based on the experimental design, feed them through the exposure mapping for each unit, and then determine each unit’s probabilities of falling into any of the exposure conditions.” p. 214 (PDF p. 6): “To compute the exposure probabilities, we first need to simulate the set of all possible (or a large random sample of all possible) treatment assignments according to the experimental design. In this case, a proportion $p = 0.1$ of the $N = 1000$ units in the network is randomly assigned to treatment with uniform probability on the basis of complete random assignment. Because the set of all possible treatment assignments is very large $\binom{N}{pN}$, we compute a set of $R$ = 10,000 random treatment assignments.” Printed calls (line breaks of the layout removed): p. 214, `possible_tr_assignment <- make_tr_vec_permutation(N, p, R = 10000, seed = 4224)`; p. 216 (PDF p. 8), `prob_exposure_sw <- make_exposure_prob(possible_tr_assignment, adj_matrix_sw, make_exposure_map_AS, list(hop = 1))`; p. 217 (PDF p. 9), `observed_tr_assignment <- make_tr_vec_permutation(N, p, R = 1, seed = 4224)`; p. 218 (PDF p. 10), `estimates_sw <- estimates(received_exposure_sw, observed_outcome_sw, prob_exposure_sw, control_condition = 'no')`, and the same calls for the second network.
(S7) Audit notation, not printed in the chapter. $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ is the exposure unit $i$ receives and $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$ its observed outcome; the exposure mapping is taken as correctly specified, $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = y_i(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i))$ for every profile. $\pi_i(d) = \Pr(D_i = d) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d)$ and $\pi_{ij}(d,e) = \Pr(D_i = d, D_j = e)$, so $\pi_{ii}(d,d) = \pi_i(d)$ and $\pi_{ii}(d,e) = 0$ for $d \ne e$. $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ are over the randomization distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ (and, where a target says so, over a simulated table of assignments); the population, the network, the mapping and the potential outcomes are fixed. The four-condition mapping is read with the treated-peer count $\theta_i\mathbf{z} = \sum_j\theta_{ij}z_j$ (P044-T9). The estimators are those computed by the staged R package interference (commit c3fc7b3; R/estimates.R and R/make_exposure_prob.R), whose documentation attributes them to Equations 1, 3, 7, 10, 11 and 15 of Aronow and Samii (2017). For marginal inputs $w_i(d) > 0$ and joint inputs $w_{ij}(d,e) \ge 0$ with $w_{ii}(d,d) = w_i(d)$, and with $I_i(d) = \mathbf{I}(D_i = d)$: [point estimator] $\widehat\mu(d) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i I_i(d)Y_i/w_i(d)$ and $\widehat\tau(k,l) = \widehat\mu(k) - \widehat\mu(l)$; [variance functional] $$\widehat V_d = \sum_{(i,j):\,w_{ij}(d,d)>0} I_i(d)I_j(d)\,Y_iY_j\left(\frac{1}{w_i(d)w_j(d)} - \frac{1}{w_{ij}(d,d)}\right) + \sum_{i\ne j:\,w_{ij}(d,d)=0}\left(\frac{I_i(d)Y_i^2}{2w_i(d)} + \frac{I_j(d)Y_j^2}{2w_j(d)}\right),$$ $$\widehat C_{kl} = \sum_{(i,j):\,w_{ij}(k,l)>0} I_i(k)I_j(l)\,Y_iY_j\left(\frac{1}{w_i(k)w_j(l)} - \frac{1}{w_{ij}(k,l)}\right) - \sum_{(i,j):\,w_{ij}(k,l)=0}\left(\frac{I_i(k)Y_i^2}{2w_i(k)} + \frac{I_j(l)Y_j^2}{2w_j(l)}\right),$$ $$\widehat V(k,l) = \frac{\widehat V_k + \widehat V_l - 2\widehat C_{kl}}{N^2},$$ all sums over ordered pairs, the first sum of $\widehat V_d$ and both sums of $\widehat C_{kl}$ including $i = j$. The exact inputs are $w = \pi$. The inputs the package returns from a table of $R$ assignments with counts $c_i(d)$ and $c_{ij}(d,e)$ are $w_i(d) = (c_i(d)+1)/(R+1)$, $w_{ij}(d,d) = c_{ij}(d,d)/(R+1)$ for $i \ne j$, and $w_{ij}(k,l) = c_{ij}(k,l)/R$ for $k \ne l$ and all $i, j$.
Scope of the list. No headline claim is a numbered result. P044-H2 (unbiasedness of the Horvitz–Thompson estimators) and P044-H4 (conservative variance estimators) are mathematical statements, and each is touched by a finding, so they enter as result_touched_by_finding targets (P044-T12, P044-T11) and there is no headline_result target. The clause of P044-H2 that Hajek or weighted least squares estimators are “consistent and considerably more efficient” is printed without hypotheses and defers to Aronow and Samii (2017), and the finding about it (P044-A002) was not confirmed; it is transcribed in P044-T12 and is not a target of its own (the formal statements belong to that paper, P013). P044-H1, H3, H9 and H10 describe the method and the package, and P044-H5 to H8 are simulation results and descriptions of the simulated networks. Six confirmed errors have corrections that change a mathematical statement and are targets: P044-N005 (Major; conservativeness of the variance estimators when the exposure probabilities are simulated), P044-E001 (Moderate; the support condition missing from the unbiasedness statement), P044-E002 (Moderate; the stated distribution of the simulated baseline outcomes), P044-E005 (Minor; the returned exposure probabilities are smoothed counts, so the implemented estimator is not exactly unbiased even with every assignment enumerated), P044-E007 (Minor; misprinted symbols in the no-interference statements and in the exposure-mapping display) and P044-E003 (Minor; the constant 0.7 for the within-community share of edges). P044-E002 and P044-E003 are descriptions of simulated inputs that disagree with the generators the printed code calls; they are listed because the correction replaces a stated distribution or constant, and each target says which premise is read from source code and lies outside what Lean can establish. The other confirmed errors are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement of the chapter: P044-E006, P044-E008 and P044-N014 (Moderate) are defects of the package code whose repair is a change of code (a missing value where a total is zero, a hard-coded control label, rejection of repeated draws in the Bernoulli samplers), and the validators find no statement of the chapter false on their account; P044-N009 (Moderate) is the scale label of the upper panel of Figure 16.3, established by re-running the simulation; P044-N004 and P044-N010 concern reproducibility; P044-N003 is a slip in reading Figure 16.1; P044-N012 is bibliographic. Findings classed as clarity notes, not confirmed or out of scope are outside the brief.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The description of the simulated potential outcomes (p. 216), corrected: the baseline is a degree-scaled absolute normal draw plus normal noise
canonical_claim.statement:
[Sol's repair (validated.json, P044-E002, sol.smallest_repair), verbatim] “Replace the second sentence with: 'Specifically, conditional on the network, we generate the baseline no-exposure outcome as B_i=(k_i+q_i+k_i q_i)|G_i|+E_i, where k_i is the first-neighbor degree, q_i counts other vertices reachable by a two-edge walk, G_i is standard normal, and E_i is normal with mean 1 and variance 1/16; these draws are independent conditional on the network.' Correct the corresponding package help description as well.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] [Setting] A 0/1 adjacency matrix $A$ on $N$ vertices with zero diagonal; $k_i = \sum_jA_{ij}$; $q_i = \#\{j\ne i : (A^2)_{ij} > 0\}$; $a_i = k_i + q_i + k_iq_i \ge 0$. Conditionally on $A$, the $2N$ random variables $G_1,\dots,G_N,E_1,\dots,E_N$ are independent with $G_i\sim N(0,1)$ and $E_i\sim N(1,1/16)$.
(i) [Corrected definition] $B_i = a_i|G_i| + E_i$; $y_i(d_{00}) = B_i$, $y_i(d_{11}) = 2B_i$, $y_i(d_{10}) = \tfrac32B_i$, $y_i(d_{01}) = \tfrac54B_i$.
(ii) [Its first two moments] $\mathrm E[B_i\mid A] = a_i\sqrt{2/\pi} + 1$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B_i\mid A) = a_i^2(1 - 2/\pi) + \tfrac1{16}$, using $\mathrm E|G_i| = \sqrt{2/\pi}$ and $\mathrm E[|G_i|^2] = 1$.
(iii) [The true effects for realized baselines] For any real numbers $B_1,\dots,B_N$ and $\bar B = \frac1N\sum_iB_i$, the outcomes in (i) give $\tau(d_{11},d_{00}) = \bar B$, $\tau(d_{10},d_{00}) = \tfrac12\bar B$ and $\tau(d_{01},d_{00}) = \tfrac14\bar B$. For the witness of P044-T5(i), $\bar B = 109/24$ and the three effects are $109/24$, $109/48$, $109/96$.
(iv) [Scale] By (ii) and (iii), $\mathrm E[\tau(d_{11},d_{00})\mid A] = 1 + \sqrt{2/\pi}\cdot\frac1N\sum_ia_i$, which is at least $1 + \sqrt{2/\pi}$ on a graph without isolates; if the baselines were distributed as $|G|$, as printed, the corresponding expectation would be $\sqrt{2/\pi} < 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P044-T5: the generator is read from R/make_dilated_out.R of the staged package (lines 108–116 and 122–150), and $N(1,1/16)$ has variance $1/16$ (standard deviation 0.25 in the code). $\tau(d,d')$ is the estimand of p. 212 (standing assumptions S5). The printed sentences that are kept: ‘The values for the other exposure conditions are obtained by multiplying a vector of multipliers by the baseline no exposure value. The multipliers take values (2,1.5,1.25) for the direct + indirect exposure, isolated direct exposure, and indirect exposure, respectively, implying positive spillover effects.’ (p. 216).
canonical_claim.note: The repair is the one settled in validated.json (prior_correction.status ‘correct’; repair cost none: the prose is corrected to describe the generator that was run, and no number changes). The correction is to a definition, so there is no theorem of the chapter to prove: the expected formalization is the definition (i) with the facts (ii)–(iv). (iii) is exact algebra and was recomputed; (ii) is the validator's section 5; (iv) follows from (ii) and (iii) by linearity and is the formal content of the remark that the described outcome law has effects below 1 where the generator's are on the scale of the degrees. That the chapter's output was produced by this generator is a premise from the staged code, as in P044-T5. ‘Implying positive spillover effects’ holds for the multipliers when $\bar B > 0$, which is not guaranteed for every draw since $B_i$ can be negative (P044-T5(ii)); that remark is not part of the finding and is not asserted here.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘These exposure probabilities are generalized propensity scores …’ and ‘the reason why we can obtain unbiased estimates’ (p. 216), for the probabilities that the package returns when it is given every assignment of the design; the witness is the first validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 216 (PDF p. 8); p. 212 (PDF p. 4) and p. 214 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact bias of the implemented Horvitz–Thompson estimator with the returned probabilities, when every assignment of the design is supplied (the first validator's witness; not in the paper).
[Setting] $N = 8$ units on the cycle with edges $\{1,2\},\{2,3\},\dots,\{7,8\},\{8,1\}$ (no isolates). Design: uniform on the eight cyclic rotations of $\mathbf z = (1,1,0,1,0,0,0,0)$, each with probability $1/8$, all other profiles with probability 0. The table supplied to the package is the complete list of these $R = 8$ assignments. Exposure mapping: the four-condition mapping. Potential outcomes, for every unit: $(y_i(d_{11}),y_i(d_{10}),y_i(d_{01}),y_i(d_{00})) = (2,\ 3/2,\ 5/4,\ 1)$, so the average potential outcomes are $(2,\ 3/2,\ 5/4,\ 1)$ and $\tau(d_{11},d_{00}) = 1$, $\tau(d_{10},d_{00}) = 1/2$, $\tau(d_{01},d_{00}) = 1/4$.
[Claims] (i) Under the base assignment the exposures of units $1,\dots,8$ are $(d_{11},d_{11},d_{01},d_{10},d_{01},d_{00},d_{00},d_{01})$. Every one of the eight assignments has 2, 1, 3, 2 units with exposures $d_{11},d_{10},d_{01},d_{00}$, and every unit has these exposures in 2, 1, 3, 2 of the eight assignments. So the exact exposure probabilities of every unit are $p = (1/4,\ 1/8,\ 3/8,\ 1/4)$, all positive. (ii) The package returns the marginal probabilities $q = \big(\tfrac{c+1}{R+1}\big) = (1/3,\ 2/9,\ 4/9,\ 1/3)$, which sum to $4/3$. (iii) With the weights $q$ the estimates $\frac1N\sum_i\mathbf I(D_i = d)Y_i/q(d)$ equal $(3/2,\ 27/32,\ 135/128,\ 3/4)$ at every one of the eight assignments, so the three contrasts with $d_{00}$ equal $(3/4,\ 3/32,\ 39/128)$ with probability one; their biases are $(-1/4,\ -13/32,\ 7/128)$. (iv) With the exact weights $p$ the estimates equal $(2,\ 3/2,\ 5/4,\ 1)$ at every assignment and the contrasts equal the targets $(1,\ 1/2,\ 1/4)$. (v) [The returned joint probabilities are not consistent with the returned marginals] The numbers of assignments with $(D_1,D_2) = (d_{11},b)$ for $b = d_{11},d_{10},d_{01},d_{00}$ are $1,0,1,0$. The returned joint entries are $1/9$ for $b = d_{11}$ and $1/8$ for $b = d_{01}$, with sum $17/72 \ne 1/3 = q_1(d_{11})$; the exact ones are $1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4 = p_1(d_{11})$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the chapter: an experimental design assigns a probability $p_{\mathbf z}$ to each profile (p. 210; standing assumptions S2); the four-condition mapping (S4); $\tau(d,d')$ (S5); ‘we first need to simulate the set of all possible (or a large random sample of all possible) treatment assignments according to the experimental design’ (p. 214; S6). Not printed in the chapter and read from the staged package: for a table of $R$ assignments with indicator matrices $I_a$ ($N\times R$, entry 1 when unit $i$ has exposure $a$ under assignment $r$), R/make_exposure_prob.R returns `(I_exposure[[i]] %*% t(I_exposure[[i]]) + diag(N)) / (R + 1)` for each exposure (line 83; its diagonal $(c_i(a)+1)/(R+1)$ is the weight used by the point estimators) and `(I_exposure[[i]] %*% t(I_exposure[[j]])) / R` for each pair of different exposures (line 88); R/estimates.R, lines 216–218 and 314, computes $\frac1N$ times the difference of the weighted totals. Every exposure group is nonempty at every assignment of the witness, so the package's replacement of an empty group's total by a missing value (P044-E006) does not arise.
canonical_claim.note: P044-E005 is rated an error, Minor. Sol's verdict: confirmed (first validator) and confirmed in part (second), both upheld on rerun; evidence an exact counterexample. The statement follows the first validator (v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–4; exact_check.py, and source_check.R, which runs the staged estimates() on all eight assignments). Everything above was recomputed by enumeration when this list was fixed. The second validator's witness is the eight rotations of $(1,1,0,0,0,1,0,0)$ on the same cycle with the same outcomes: exposure counts $(2,1,4,1)$, estimated contrasts $(15/16,\ 9/32,\ 9/16)$ at every assignment, biases $(-1/16,\ -7/32,\ 5/16)$ (v2/artifact/derivation.md); also recomputed. The unbiasedness of the Horvitz–Thompson estimator with the true probabilities is not in question (P044-T4(a)); what fails is the identification of the returned numbers with the design's exposure probabilities. Not established: the size of the effect on the chapter's estimates from 10,000 draws; the rating records it as small in the chapter's setting. The Hajek contrasts equal the targets in this witness, because the outcomes are constant within each exposure.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The exposure probabilities of the recipe (pp. 212, 214, 216), corrected: exact unbiasedness holds for the true positive design probabilities, which for an exhaustive equally likely list are counts divided by $R$; the returned smoothed values are approximations
canonical_claim.location: p. 216 (PDF p. 8); p. 212 (PDF p. 4) and p. 214 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text (validated.json, P044-E005, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Horvitz–Thompson estimators are exactly unbiased when weighted by true positive design exposure probabilities. In the displayed example those probabilities are approximated from a finite bank of simulated assignments using smoothed weights, so exact finite-bank unbiasedness is not guaranteed. For exhaustive equally likely assignment enumeration use I_d I_d^T/R for same-exposure probabilities and I_d I_e^T/R for cross-exposure probabilities, with R the number of assignments.”
[Sol's repair (sol.smallest_repair), verbatim] “For exhaustive equally likely input return I_d I_d^T/R for every same-exposure matrix; cross-exposure matrices already use the correct counts/R. Apply the corresponding counts/R change to the separate marginal calculation if the batch interface is used. Reserve exact HT unbiasedness for true positive design exposure probabilities. For the chapter's finite random-bank workflow, state that the probabilities and inverse weights are numerical approximations, describe the smoothing, and remove the implication of guaranteed exact finite-bank unbiasedness.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] [Setting] A design that is uniform on a list $\mathbf z_1,\dots,\mathbf z_R$ of $R$ distinct profiles (every assignment of the design, equally likely); an exposure mapping with $K$ mutually exclusive and exhaustive exposures; counts $c_i(a) = \#\{r : f(\mathbf z_r,\theta_i) = a\}$ and $c_{ij}(a,b) = \#\{r : f(\mathbf z_r,\theta_i) = a,\ f(\mathbf z_r,\theta_j) = b\}$; fixed real potential outcomes; $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$.
(i) [Exact probabilities from an exhaustive list] $\pi_i(a) = c_i(a)/R$ and $\pi_{ij}(a,b) = c_{ij}(a,b)/R$ for all units and exposures, including $a = b$; in matrix form $I_aI_a^{\mathsf T}/R$ and $I_aI_b^{\mathsf T}/R$.
(ii) [Expectation with arbitrary fixed weights] For fixed weights $w_i(a) > 0$, $\mathrm E\!\left[\frac1N\sum_i\frac{\mathbf I(D_i = a)Y_i}{w_i(a)}\right] = \frac1N\sum_iy_i(a)\frac{\pi_i(a)}{w_i(a)}$. With $w_i(a) = \pi_i(a) > 0$ for every $i$ this is $\frac1N\sum_iy_i(a)$: the estimator is exactly unbiased.
(iii) [The returned weights] With $w_i(a) = q_i(a) = \frac{c_i(a)+1}{R+1}$: $\frac{\pi_i(a)}{q_i(a)} - 1 = \frac{c_i(a) - R}{R\,(c_i(a)+1)}$, so the bias of the estimated average potential outcome is $\frac1N\sum_iy_i(a)\frac{c_i(a)-R}{R\,(c_i(a)+1)}$, in which the multiplier of $y_i(a)$ is negative whenever $c_i(a) < R$. Moreover $\sum_aq_i(a) = \frac{R+K}{R+1} > 1$ for $K \ge 2$, so the returned marginal values are not a probability distribution over the exposures.
(iv) [A finite random bank, for illustration] If the bank consists of $R$ independent draws from the design (with replacement), independent of the realized assignment, and $C \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(R,p)$ is the number of draws in which a unit with exposure probability $p \in (0,1)$ has exposure $a$, then with $q = (C+1)/(R+1)$: $\mathrm E[\mathbf I(D = a)/q] = 1 - (1-p)^{R+1} < 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The setting, the recipe and $\tau(d,d')$ are in the standing assumptions (S1–S6); $D_i$, $Y_i$, $\pi_i$, $\pi_{ij}$ in S7. $I_a$ is the $N\times R$ matrix with entry 1 when unit $i$ has exposure $a$ under the $r$-th listed assignment (the package's I_exposure). The returned values $q$ are those of R/make_exposure_prob.R, lines 83 and 88 (same-exposure matrix $(I_aI_a^{\mathsf T} + \mathrm{diag}(N))/(R+1)$, cross-exposure matrix $I_aI_b^{\mathsf T}/R$). In (iv) the assumptions (draws with replacement, independent of the realized assignment) are the validator's, for illustration; the chapter's bank is drawn without replacement and shares its seed with the realized assignment (pp. 214 and 217), so (iv) is not a calculation of the bias in the chapter's example.
canonical_claim.note: The repair is the one settled in validated.json (prior_correction.status ‘correct’; second validator's repair to the same effect; repair cost recorded as a weaker conclusion for the finite-bank workflow, none for the exhaustive case). (i)–(iii) are sections 1–2 of the first validator's derivation and (iv) its section 6, where the identity is derived from $\frac{R+1}{c+1}\binom{R}{c} = \binom{R+1}{c+1}$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The no-interference and interference statements and the four-condition exposure-mapping display (p. 211), with the misprinted symbols corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 211 (PDF p. 3); the vector convention on p. 210 (PDF p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 210 (PDF p. 2)] The $N \times 1$ vector of treatments for all units is given by $\mathbf{z} = (z_1,...,z_N)'$. [Printed, p. 211 (PDF p. 3)] Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (...,z_{i-1},z_{i+1},...)$ denote the $(N-1)$-element vector that removes the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. Then we can also denote unit $i$’s potential outcome as $y_i(z_i;\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. This allows us to characterize how effects for unit $i$ might occur through direct exposure to the treatment (i.e., through variation in $z_i$, keeping $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ fixed) or indirect spillovers (i.e., through variation in $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$, keeping $z_i$ fixed). Traditional analyses of experiments assume no interference, which would imply that unit $i$’s outcome depends only on the element $z_i$; that is, for any $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, $y_i(z_i;\mathbf{z}) = y_i(z_i;\mathbf{z}')$. Interference means for some unit $i \in U$ we have $y_i(z_i;\mathbf{z}) \ne y_i(z_i;\mathbf{z}')$. [The exposure-mapping display of p. 211 is transcribed in the standing assumptions (S4); its four conditions are $z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1$, $z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1$, $(1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1$, $(1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1$, with $\theta_i$ described as ‘unit $i$’s row in the adjacency matrix’.]
[Sol's repair (validated.json, P044-E007, sol.smallest_repair), verbatim] “For all $i$, $a\in\{0,1\}$, and $\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in\{0,1\}^{N-1}$, no interference means $y_i(a;\mathbf u)=y_i(a;\mathbf v)$; interference means that there exist $i,a,\mathbf u,\mathbf v$ for which these differ. Retain $\theta_i$ as the ith row and replace $\mathbf z\prime\theta_i$ by $\theta_i\mathbf z$ in all four exposure conditions.”
[Mathematical content] [Setting] $N \ge 1$; $y_i : \{0,1\}^N \to \mathbb R$ for each $i \in U$; for $a \in \{0,1\}$ and $\mathbf u \in \{0,1\}^{N-1}$ let $(a;\mathbf u)_i$ be the profile whose $i$th entry is $a$ and whose other entries are those of $\mathbf u$ in order, and $y_i(a;\mathbf u) = y_i((a;\mathbf u)_i)$, so that $y_i(z_i;\mathbf z_{-i}) = y_i(\mathbf z)$; $\theta$ an $N\times N$ matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ and zero diagonal, $\theta_i$ its $i$th row.
(i) [Corrected definitions] No interference: for all $i \in U$, $a \in \{0,1\}$ and $\mathbf u,\mathbf v \in \{0,1\}^{N-1}$, $y_i(a;\mathbf u) = y_i(a;\mathbf v)$. Interference: there exist $i \in U$, $a \in \{0,1\}$ and $\mathbf u,\mathbf v \in \{0,1\}^{N-1}$ with $y_i(a;\mathbf u) \ne y_i(a;\mathbf v)$. Interference holds if and only if no interference fails. No interference is equivalent to: for all $i$ and all profiles $\mathbf z$, $\mathbf z'$ with $z_i = z'_i$, $y_i(\mathbf z) = y_i(\mathbf z')$.
(ii) [The treated-peer count] With $\mathbf z$ an $N\times1$ column and $\theta_i$ a $1\times N$ row, $\theta_i\mathbf z = \sum_{j=1}^N\theta_{ij}z_j$ is a scalar, the number of units $j$ with $\theta_{ij} = 1$ and $z_j = 1$; because $\theta_{ii} = 0$ it does not depend on $z_i$. The printed $\mathbf z'\theta_i$ is a product of a $1\times N$ row with a $1\times N$ row, which is not defined for $N > 1$.
(iii) [Corrected display] $$f(\mathbf z,\theta_i) = \begin{cases} d_{11}: & z_i\mathbf I(\theta_i\mathbf z > 0) = 1,\\ d_{10}: & z_i\mathbf I(\theta_i\mathbf z = 0) = 1,\\ d_{01}: & (1-z_i)\mathbf I(\theta_i\mathbf z > 0) = 1,\\ d_{00}: & (1-z_i)\mathbf I(\theta_i\mathbf z = 0) = 1.\end{cases}$$ For every $\mathbf z \in \{0,1\}^N$ and every $i$ exactly one of the four conditions holds, so $f(\cdot,\theta_i)$ is a well-defined function from $\{0,1\}^N$ to $\{d_{11},d_{10},d_{01},d_{00}\}$, with $f(\mathbf z,\theta_i) = d_{ab}$ for $a = z_i$ and $b = \mathbf I(\theta_i\mathbf z > 0)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: All objects are those of the standing assumptions (S1–S4). In the printed statements the four second arguments $\mathbf z$ and $\mathbf z'$ of $y_i(z_i;\cdot)$ should be $(N-1)$-element vectors of the other units' treatments, as in the definition of $y_i(z_i;\mathbf z_{-i})$ two sentences earlier. The prime is used in the chapter both for the transpose ($\mathbf z = (z_1,...,z_N)'$) and for a second profile ($\mathbf z'$); in the display it is the transpose.
canonical_claim.note: P044-E007 is rated an error, Minor: misprinted symbols that a reader corrects from the definitions just above; nothing depends on them (Sol: confirmed, false as printed, not false under the natural reading, repair cost none, evidence a complete derivation in the batch validation, section E007 of the cited file). The correction is to two definitions, so there is no theorem of the chapter to prove: the expected formalization is the definitions in (i) and (iii) with the two equivalences of (i), the scalar identity of (ii) and the exactly-one property of (iii). The exactly-one property is not printed in the chapter; it is what makes the corrected display a definition, and Sol records it among the points that held up (the four categories partition the assignments when the adjacency matrix has a zero diagonal). The statement that the printed product is not conformable is a remark about matrix dimensions and need not be formalized. The existential quantifier over the other units' assignments in the interference statement is implicit in the printed sentence; Sol does not count its absence as a separate defect. The double use of the prime is P044-N002 (not confirmed) and is not part of this target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘an expected proportion of edges that is within a community of 0.7’ (p. 214), corrected for the generator call printed on p. 215: every edge is within a community
canonical_claim.location: p. 214 (PDF p. 6); code on p. 215 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, pp. 213–214 (PDF pp. 5–6)] The second network we construct is a degree-corrected stochastic block model (DCBM) (Karrer & Newman, 2011), featuring relatively high-clustering, but more variation in vertex degree than is possible to produce with small-world networks. In particular, we generate a network according to a DCBM with $N = 1000$ units, 10 communities (or clusters); where units are assigned to one of the 10 communities uniformly at random, and an expected proportion of edges that is within a community of 0.7. The expected average degree in this network is 10 (as with the small-world network), and the variance is 75 (compared to a variance of 2 in the small-world network). [Printed code, p. 215 (PDF p. 7), layout line breaks removed] `make_adj_matrix_dcsbm <- function(N, seed) { set.seed(seed); g <- randnet::BlockModel.Gen(10, N, K=10, rho = 0.7, alpha = 1); while (min(rowSums(g$A)) == 0) { g <- randnet::BlockModel.Gen(10, N, K=10, rho = 0.7, alpha = 1) }; return(g$A) }` and `adj_matrix_dcbm <- make_adj_matrix_dcsbm(N, seed = 42)`.
[Sol's repair, as settled by the external source check (runs/P044/settle/settled.json, P044-E003, smallest_repair), verbatim] “Replace the within-community proportion 0.7 with 1 (all edges within communities). Explain separately that rho=0.7 controls low degree weights before the no-isolates rejection. Keeping 70% as the edge-share target would require changing the generator settings and regenerating the numerical example.”
[Mathematical content] [Premise, read from the source of randnet and not part of the formal statement] With the defaults `beta = 0` and `simple = TRUE` that the printed call leaves in force, the generator draws a simple undirected graph on $N$ vertices with independent edges of probabilities $p_{ij} = s\,t_it_j\,P_{c_ic_j}$ for $i < j$, where $c_i \in \{1,\dots,K\}$ is the community of vertex $i$, $t_i$ is its degree weight ($t_i = 1/5$ with probability $\rho = 7/10$ and $t_i = 1$ otherwise, independently), $s \ge 0$ is a normalizing constant and $P$ is the $K\times K$ identity matrix.
[Statement] (i) If $c_i \ne c_j$ then $p_{ij} = 0$; hence, with probability one, the graph has no edge between vertices of different communities. (ii) A simple undirected graph on $N \ge 1$ vertices in which every vertex has positive degree has $M \ge N/2 > 0$ edges, since the degrees sum to $2M$. (iii) Therefore every graph returned by the printed loop, which accepts a draw only when no row sum is zero, has $W = M > 0$, where $M$ is its number of edges and $W$ its number of edges within a community: the within-community proportion $W/M$ equals 1 for every returned graph. Consequently $\mathrm E[W/M] = 1$ and $\mathrm E[W]/\mathrm E[M] = 1$ over returned graphs, against the printed 0.7, a difference of $3/10$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The network is the $N\times N$ adjacency matrix of the standing assumptions (S1); Note 1 (p. 221): ‘Our networks do not have isolates, but we suggest researchers remove isolates from their analysis.’ ‘Proportion of edges that is within a community’ is read as $W/M$ for a realized graph; the two expectations in (iii) cover both readings of ‘expected proportion’. The premise is from the source of randnet 0.5 (R/RCode.R, line 9: `BlockModel.Gen <- function(lambda,n,beta=0,K=3,w=rep(1,K),Pi=rep(1,K)/K,rho=0,simple=TRUE,power=TRUE,alpha=5,degree.seed=NULL){`; line 10: `P0 <- diag(w)`; line 22: `node.degree <- rep(1,n)`; line 25: `node.degree[runif(n)<rho] <- 0.2`), as quoted in runs/P044/settle/settled.json; that package is not staged with the chapter.
canonical_claim.note: The most marginal target on the list. P044-E003 is rated an error, Minor: a constant in the description of the second example network, with no estimate or comparison depending on it. The validator could not decide it without the generator's source (verdict undetermined; its derivation gives the conditional mathematics, steps 1–6, used above); an external source check then read the randnet source, re-ran the printed code, and confirmed the finding (runs/P044/settle/settled.json: the regenerated graph has within-community share 1, ten connected components, a low-weight fraction of 0.723, degree variance 75.87 and skewness 1.075, and reproduces the twelve DCBM numbers printed on p. 218). The mathematics is elementary once the premise is granted, and the premise is a fact about software that Lean cannot establish; the target is listed because the correction replaces a printed constant and the author's instruction covers every such error at any severity. If nothing beyond (i)–(iii) can be stated, a short formalization of (ii) and (iii) for a graph with no edge between communities is the whole of it. Not asserted: that exactly 70% of the vertices of the accepted graph have the low weight (the rejection of graphs with isolates changes that distribution), or that the accepted graph has exactly ten components in general.
